title: Arti at home

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhya, the hour where two things join. Your line was the junction.

On the banks of the Ganga at dusk, priests stand in a row, each holding up a huge brass lamp with a crown of flames, swinging it in slow circles as bells clang and thousands of people sing. The river turns gold. It's one of the most famous sights in India, and maybe you've seen it in videos. Now shrink it. A kitchen. A shelf. One small plate with one small flame, held by someone in socks, and maybe a kid ringing a bell a little too hard. Same act.
screen: `THE GANGA AT DUSK, LAMPS BLAZING.` → `NOW SHRINK IT.` → `ONE PLATE, ONE FLAME, AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Arti was your fourteenth word, way back in camp one: light passed hand to hand. That was what it means; today is how it's done. The word comes from the Sanskrit aratrika, often explained as a rite done at night, or one that removes darkness. At home, the lamp is usually a small plate with a ghee wick, or a piece of camphor that burns bright and fast. You stand before the image and move the flame in slow circles, clockwise. Many people make a pattern: a few circles at the feet, a few at the middle, a few at the face, then around the whole form. Families do it in different ways, and there's no single count everyone agrees on. While the flame circles, a bell rings, in your other hand or someone else's. And there's singing: an arti song, which you'll learn tomorrow. Why circle? People give a few answers. You circle what's at the center of your life, so a flame circled before the image puts the divine at the center. It also lets the light fall on every part of the form, as if you were seeing all of it by lamplight. And people often point out that camphor burns without leaving any ash behind. Some say that's the whole hope of devotion: burn bright, give light, and leave no ego behind.
screen: `ARTI — FROM ARATRIKA.` · `A SMALL FLAME, CIRCLED CLOCKWISE.` · `FEET, MIDDLE, FACE, THE WHOLE.` · `CAMPHOR LEAVES NO ASH.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or small lamp and it's safe, light it and hold it steady on a plate in your right hand; if not, use your open hand, or just your eyes. Before an image, a photo or simply a window, make a few slow circles clockwise, a few low, a few in the middle, a few at the height of a face, slowly enough to watch the light move. Then set it down and sit with the flame.
Camphor, the flame that burns bright and leaves no ash: circled clockwise at home in front of the image, with a bell and a song, so the light falls on every part. Today's word.
Your line: light, circled. What you circle, you put at the center. That's day one hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: At home, many Hindus perform arti at dawn and at dusk by circling a small ghee lamp or burning camphor clockwise before the image, often in a pattern from the feet to the face, while a bell is rung and an arti song is sung.

chat.says: Why do people move the little flame in circles in front of the image?
options: Circling puts the divine at the center, and lets light fall on every part.
To keep the flame from going out while everyone sings the song.
To fan the smoke away from the image so it stays clean.
